canonical_name: EMIR — Regulation (EU) No 648/2012 on OTC Derivatives
description: European Market Infrastructure Regulation. Requires central clearing of standardised OTC derivatives, bilateral margin requirements for non-cleared derivatives, and trade reporting to trade repositories. Cleared through CCPs.

EMIR REFIT amends EMIR to proportionate the clearing obligation and reporting requirements, particularly for smaller counterparties. Introduces the distinction between Financial Counterparties above/below clearing threshold and Non-Financial Counterparties.
EMIR 3.0 amends EMIR and EMIR REFIT to reduce reliance on third-country CCPs (particularly LCH London post-Brexit), promote EU clearing market, and address active account requirements. In force 2024.

Regulation on transparency of securities financing transactions. Requires reporting of repos, securities lending, buy-sell-backs, and margin lending to trade repositories. Mandatory publication of collateral re-use information.

A financial market infrastructure that interposes itself between counterparties to contracts traded in financial markets. CCPs manage counterparty credit risk through clearing, netting, and collateral. CCPs are authorised entities under EMIR. AML: CCPs process large volumes of derivatives transactions.

Central entity that centrally collects and maintains records of OTC derivatives (EMIR) and SFTs (SFTR). TRs are registered with ESMA. Regulators access TR data for systemic risk monitoring. AML investigators use TR data for derivatives exposure analysis.

Collateral posted to manage counterparty credit risk. Initial margin: posted at inception of trade. Variation margin: daily mark-to-market settlements. Mandatory for both cleared and non-cleared OTC derivatives. AML risk: margin calls/disputes can mask value transfers.

Assets posted as security to manage credit exposure. Eligibility criteria defined by CCPs and EMIR. Types: government bonds, cash, equities. Collateral re-use (rehypothecation) disclosure required under SFTR.

Short-term borrowing mechanism where securities are sold with agreement to repurchase at a specified price and date. Used for collateral management and short-term funding. AML risk: repos can be used to move value or create fictitious transactions.

Temporary transfer of securities from lender to borrower against collateral. Borrower must return equivalent securities. Covered by SFTR reporting. AML risk: securities lending can facilitate short-selling and dividend stripping schemes.

A financial contract whose value is derived from an underlying asset, traded bilaterally (over-the-counter) rather than on an exchange. EMIR requires reporting of all OTC derivatives. Standardised OTC derivatives must be centrally cleared.

EMIR obligation requiring certain OTC derivatives to be cleared through authorised CCPs. Applies to Financial Counterparties (FCs) and Non-Financial Counterparties above the clearing threshold (NFC+). Interest rate swaps and credit default swaps in scope.

Counterparty type under EMIR including investment firms, credit institutions, insurance companies, UCITs, and alternative investment funds. FCs are always subject to the clearing obligation (if above threshold). All FCs are typically obliged entities under AMLR.

Counterparty type under EMIR for non-financial corporates using derivatives for hedging. NFC+ (above clearing threshold) subject to clearing obligation; NFC- (below threshold) exempt but still must report. Different from NFC's AMLR status.

EMIR Art. 9 requires all counterparties to OTC derivatives contracts (and since EMIR REFIT, also ETDs) to report to a trade repository no later than T+1. Reports include: counterparty data, contract type, clearing status, margin, collateral.

EMIR 3.0 requirement for EU firms to hold active clearing accounts at EU-authorised CCPs for systemically important derivatives classes. Aims to reduce dependency on UK CCPs (LCH) for euro-denominated derivatives following Brexit.

CCPs and investment firms operating in derivatives markets are obliged entities under AMLR. CCP clearing membership criteria must include AML/CFT checks. Margin and collateral flows monitored under AML transaction monitoring. SFTR reporting used in ML investigations.

CCPs are subject to DORA digital operational resilience requirements in addition to EMIR. CCPs identified as critical financial market infrastructure must comply with DORA ICT risk management, incident reporting, and resilience testing requirements.

Both EMIR Art.9 (derivatives trade reporting) and MiFIR Art.26 (transaction reporting) may require reporting of the same derivative transaction. EMIR captures notional/risk data; MiFIR captures price/execution data. Both serve regulatory surveillance purposes.

Process by which a CCP interposes itself between buyer and seller of a derivatives contract: (1) Trade submitted for clearing; (2) CCP accepts/rejects; (3) Original contract novated to CCP; (4) CCP manages margin calls; (5) Settlement. AML: clearing memberships must be AML-checked.

Process for reporting SFTs to trade repositories: counterparties report by T+1; report fields include: counterparty data, principal amount, collateral, haircut, repo rate, maturity. Counterparties may delegate reporting to the other party or a third party (delegated reporting).

ESMA directly supervises trade repositories under EMIR and SFTR. ESMA also authorises and supervises non-EU CCPs (Tier 1 and Tier 2) recognised under EMIR. Issues binding technical standards on reporting and clearing.

Margin disputes and unexpected margin calls can be used as a cover for transferring funds. ML typology: criminals may use derivatives positions and margin flows to layer proceeds. Unexplained margin payments or frequent position unwinding are AML red flags.
